name: SafeStep PocketGuard OC-1
description:
The SafeStep PocketGuard OC-1 is the most ubiquitous self-defense product in GLMZ's lower tiers — a palm-sized aerosol canister containing a 1.2% oleoresin capsicum suspension in a water-glycol carrier. It is sold in vending machines across the Shelf alongside nutrient bars and bootleg sim-patches, requiring no license and no identification. The canister is injection-molded from recycled polymer in a standardized red-and-grey livery, with a thumb-actuated nozzle guard to prevent accidental discharge in a pocket or bag. Shelf life is rated at eighteen months, though most units cycle through their owners in far less time.

The OC-1 produces a short-range cone spray effective to approximately 1.5 meters, causing immediate lacrimation, mucosal irritation, and temporary vision impairment in unaugmented targets. It is emphatically not designed for augmented opponents — those with sealed ocular implants or respiratory filters will experience minimal effect. SafeStep's own product literature acknowledges this limitation with the phrase 'optimized for unaugmented personal safety scenarios,' which on the Shelf is understood to mean 'works on other Shelf residents and not much else.'

Despite its limitations, the OC-1 is considered a civic staple. Municipal aid organizations distribute them in bulk during social unrest cycles. Social workers carry them. Children are given them by parents who cannot afford anything better. The product has been manufactured in essentially the same form for forty years, with SafeStep updating only the canister color and the compliance text on the label.
legality: Legal — no license required, unrestricted civilian sale including vending machine distribution
specifications:
Active agent: 1.2% oleoresin capsicum (OC)
Carrier: water-glycol suspension
Net weight: 42g
Canister material: recycled injection-molded polymer
Nozzle type: thumb-guard cone spray
Effective range: 0.5–1.5m
Spray duration: approx. 6 seconds continuous
Shelf life: 18 months
Price: Φ5
tactical_use: Deployed at close range during muggings, domestic disputes, and opportunistic attacks. Users are advised to spray toward the face and eyes of an unaugmented attacker and immediately create distance. The OC-1 is a deterrent and an escape tool, not a fighting weapon — it buys seconds, not victories. In confined spaces such as stairwells or transit pods, blowback onto the user is a significant risk, as the cone pattern disperses widely.
cultural_context: On the Shelf, the OC-1 is called 'the red can' or simply 'shelf spray.' Carrying one is so normalized it carries no stigma whatsoever — it is as unremarkable as a transit card. Street wisdom holds that 'a red can won't stop chrome, but chrome doesn't usually bother with you' — a resigned acknowledgment of the product's limitations against augmented threats. Teenagers modify the nozzle guards with colored tape or stickers as a form of personalization. Finding an empty canister on the ground is considered a bad omen for the block.
story_hooks: A child presses a battered OC-1 into the player's hands before they descend into a building where the child's parent was taken — it's the only weapon the family owns.
